title: Metrizable profinite quotients through which a metric-valued function factors
statement: Let $S$ be a profinite space (compact Hausdorff with a basis of clopen sets), let $G$ be a profinite group (compact Hausdorff with a basis of open normal subgroups), let $r\geq1$ be an integer, and let $(Y,d_Y)$ be a metric space, with no completeness hypothesis. For every continuous $f:S\times G^r\to Y$ there exist a metrizable profinite space $S_0$, a metrizable profinite group $G_0$, continuous surjections $p:S\to S_0$ and $q:G\to G_0$, with $q$ a group homomorphism, and a continuous $f_0:S_0\times G_0^r\to Y$ such that $f=f_0\circ(p\times q^r)$. The empty $S$ is allowed. All spaces use [def-weil-size-convention].

source.place: Paragraph (3), scalar tame-kernel expansion: metrizable reduction of one continuous cocycle, without completing its values; agent-formulated auxiliary lemma, exact literature reference WANTED.

proof.text: If $S=\varnothing$, take $S_0=\varnothing$ with its unique topology and empty metric, $G_0=\{1\}$ with its discrete group topology, and the unique maps $p,q,f_0$. These are continuous and $p,q$ are surjective, $q$ is a homomorphism, and the required identity has empty domain. Thus assume $S\ne\varnothing$ for the remaining steps.

source.place: Paragraph (3), agent expansion of the metrizable reduction: empty parameter space

proof.text: Write $D=S\times G^r$. It is compact by [lem-weil-pbc-tychonoff-product-quasi-compact], applied to its finitely many compact factors. Fix $\epsilon>0$. For each $x=(s,g_1,\ldots,g_r)\in D$, continuity gives a product neighbourhood mapping into $B_Y(f(x),\epsilon/3)$. Using the clopen basis of $S$ and the open-normal-subgroup basis of $G$, shrink it to a rectangle $U_x\times g_1H_x\times\cdots\times g_rH_x$, where $U_x$ is clopen and $H_x$ is open normal (intersect the finitely many subgroups chosen for the coordinates). Cosets are open; they are closed because their complements are unions of other open cosets. Any two values on this rectangle have distance less than $2\epsilon/3$, by the triangle inequality.

source.place: Paragraph (3), agent expansion of the metrizable reduction: small-oscillation product neighbourhoods

proof.text: Choose finitely many such rectangles $R_j=U_j\times a_{j,1}H_j\times\cdots\times a_{j,r}H_j$ covering $D$, by compactness. Let $\mathcal P$ consist of the nonempty Boolean atoms of the finitely many clopens $U_j$: intersections choosing $U_j$ or its complement for every $j$. It is a finite clopen partition. Put $N=\bigcap_jH_j$, an open normal subgroup. If $s,s^\prime$ belong to the same atom and $g_iN=g_i^\prime N$ for every $i$, choose $R_j$ containing $(s,g_1,\ldots,g_r)$. The same atom lies in $U_j$, and $g_i^\prime=g_in_i$ for some $n_i\in N\subseteq H_j$. Thus $(s^\prime,g_1^\prime,\ldots,g_r^\prime)$ also lies in $R_j$, and the two $f$-values have distance less than $\epsilon$. This is the required uniform oscillation bound, directly from the finite cover.

source.place: Paragraph (3), agent expansion of the metrizable reduction: finite Boolean refinement and one normal subgroup for all coordinates

proof.text: For every integer $n\geq0$, perform the preceding construction with $\epsilon_n=2^{-n}$, obtaining $\mathcal P_n,N_n$. Let $A_n$ be the finite discrete set of atoms of $\mathcal P_n$, and let $B_n=G/N_n$ with its discrete topology and quotient group law. The set $B_n$ is finite: its open cosets cover compact $G$, so a finite subcover includes every coset. The maps $p_n:S\to A_n$ and $q_n:G\to B_n$ are continuous surjections, since each point fibre is a clopen atom or open coset; $q_n$ is a homomorphism by normality. Their common product fibres satisfy the distance bound $d_Y(f(s,g),f(s^\prime,g^\prime))<2^{-n}$. Neither nesting the partitions nor completing $Y$ is needed.

source.place: Paragraph (3), agent expansion of the metrizable reduction: a sequence of finite space and group quotients

proof.text: Define $P:S\to\prod_{n\geq0}A_n$ by $P(s)=(p_n(s))_n$, and $Q:G\to\prod_{n\geq0}B_n$ by $Q(g)=(q_n(g))_n$. Set $S_0=P(S)$ and $G_0=Q(G)$ with their subspace topologies [def-kun-subspace-topology], and corestrict $P,Q$ to surjections $p,q$. Preimages of basic cylinders are finite intersections of coordinate preimages, so $P,Q,p,q$ are continuous. By [lem-weil-pbc-continuous-image-quasi-compact], both images are compact. Each product, and each image, is Hausdorff: unequal tuples differ in a coordinate, whose disjoint singleton cylinders separate them. Basic cylinders specify finitely many coordinates and are clopen; their intersections with $S_0$ form a clopen basis. Consequently $S_0$ is profinite in exactly the sense of the statement.

source.place: Paragraph (3), agent expansion of the metrizable reduction: compact images of the diagonal coordinate maps

proof.text: The image $G_0$ is a subgroup of $\prod_nB_n$: $Q(gh)=Q(g)Q(h)$, $Q(g^{-1})=Q(g)^{-1}$, and $Q(1)=1$. Thus $q$ is a homomorphism. Componentwise multiplication and inversion on the product are continuous, since preimages of finite-coordinate cylinders are open, and their restrictions give continuous operations on $G_0$. For a finite set $F\subseteq\mathbf N$, put $K_F=\{b\in G_0:b_n=1\text{ for all }n\in F\}$. These are open normal subgroups, being finite intersections of coordinate kernels, and they form a neighbourhood basis of $1$: every basic cylinder neighbourhood of $1$ contains one of them. With compactness and Hausdorffness from the preceding step, this proves that $G_0$ is a profinite group under the definition in the item.

source.place: Paragraph (3), agent expansion of the metrizable reduction: the group image and its open normal neighbourhood basis

proof.text: Give each finite set $A_n,B_n$ its discrete metric, with distance $0$ on equal points and $1$ otherwise. The coordinate maps on $S_0$ and on $G_0$ are continuous and separate distinct tuples, and these two image spaces are compact. Apply [lem-sfb-compact-countable-separating-metrizable] to each of these two sequences of coordinate maps. It follows that both $S_0$ and $G_0$ are metrizable. No metric on the original $S$ or $G$ is assumed.

source.place: Paragraph (3), agent expansion of the metrizable reduction: metrizable compact images from countably many separating coordinates

proof.text: Let $R=p\times q^r:D\to S_0\times G_0^r$. If $R(s,g_1,\ldots,g_r)=R(s^\prime,g_1^\prime,\ldots,g_r^\prime)$, equality of every $n$th coordinate implies $p_n(s)=p_n(s^\prime)$ and $q_n(g_i)=q_n(g_i^\prime)$ for all $i$. Step 4 gives $d_Y(f(s,g),f(s^\prime,g^\prime))<2^{-n}$ for every $n$. Since $2^{-n}\to0$ and distances are nonnegative, this distance is zero, and the metric separation axiom gives equality of the two values. Hence $f$ is constant on each fibre of $R$.

source.place: Paragraph (3), agent expansion of the metrizable reduction: vanishing of the distance on a common quotient fibre

proof.text: The map $R$ is continuous by its coordinate formula. It is surjective: for a point $(s_0,b_1,\ldots,b_r)$ choose a preimage of $s_0$ under $p$ and, independently, a preimage of each $b_i$ under $q$. Its domain $D$ is compact by step 2, and its codomain is Hausdorff by coordinate separation. Apply [lem-sfb-compact-hausdorff-surjection-quotient] (with the whole spaces as the two subsets): $R$ is a quotient map, so a subset $W$ of its codomain is open precisely when $R^{-1}(W)$ is open.

source.place: Paragraph (3), agent expansion of the metrizable reduction: quotient topology for the product surjection

proof.text: Define $f_0(t)$ to be the common value of $f$ on the nonempty fibre $R^{-1}(t)$. Steps 8 and 9 make this well-defined and give $f=f_0\circ R$. For any open $V\subseteq Y$, one has $R^{-1}(f_0^{-1}(V))=f^{-1}(V)$, which is open. The quotient criterion in step 9 therefore makes $f_0^{-1}(V)$ open, proving continuity. The values are actual values of $f$ in $Y$, so this argument does not require completeness. Under [def-weil-size-convention], finite partitions, finite quotients, countable products and their image subsets remain in the chosen universe, as do the constructed maps. This supplies every required object and identity.

source.place: Paragraph (3), agent expansion of the metrizable reduction: continuous descent with values in the original metric space and the size convention
